title: Ansel and the Letter
premise: In 1893, apprentice clockmaker Paloma Fairweather—known to the observatory as Ansel, the name on his forged papers—is summoned to repair the great master clock and keep his head down. But when a sealed letter hidden in the clock's case reveals that his employer's family conspired with a corrupt magistrate to falsify land claims and displace a river settlement, Ansel realizes the letter also names 'the boy called Ansel' as an unwitting witness they intend to silence. Over three days he must smuggle the evidence past three checkpoints—the gatehouse, the mail coach, and the magistrate's own clerk—to reach a sympathetic journalist in the city, while deciding whether the found family of fellow servants will risk everything beside him. The story ends at the third checkpoint, where Ansel trades the letter for his own exposure: he testifies under his true name, loses his forged identity and his trade, but gains a real family among the displaced settlers, while the master clock, left unrepaired, stops—a public symbol of the family's fallen power.
about_author: Paloma Montrose is the pen name of a former museum conservator who spent years restoring Victorian timepieces before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about quiet people caught in loud histories.

chapters.title: The Boy Called Ansel
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Summoned to Thornfield Observatory under his forged name, Paloma navigates the household's hierarchy, mending the master clock's escapement while cataloguing exits and alliances among the servants. He befriends cook's assistant Maren and stable boy Ivo, forming the first threads of belonging. Emotional beat: cautious hope shadowed by the constant fear of discovery.

chapters.title: Escapement
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Working inside the clock's housing, Paloma finds a sealed letter wedged behind the strike train, addressed to no one and signed with the magistrate's seal. He reads enough to understand it implicates the Fairweather-adjacent Ashcombe family in forged river-land claims—and names him as a loose end. Emotional beat: vertigo; the safe invisibility he built begins collapsing.

chapters.title: What the House Knows
chapters.summary: POV Maren. Through Maren's eyes we see the servants' quiet economy of secrets: she has suspected the Ashcombes for years after her brother was evicted from the river settlement. She notices Ansel's changed manner and offers an oblique warning without asking questions. Emotional beat: two wary people recognizing each other as allies.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Paloma maps his route: the gatehouse where guards log every departure, the Tuesday mail coach, and the magistrate's clerk who inspects outgoing parcels. He rehearses cover stories with Ivo's help and hides the letter inside a broken pendulum bob. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into purpose; the apprentice becomes a planner.

chapters.title: The Master's Dinner
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. At a formal dinner, Paloma serves as clock-minder and overhears Mr. Ashcombe and the magistrate discussing the settlement's final eviction date—three days hence—and a mention of 'the clock boy.' Paloma realizes they know a witness exists but not who. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into resolve; the countdown begins.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Gatehouse
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. Ivo creates a diversion—a lame horse, a staged quarrel—so Paloma can slip toward the village with the pendulum bob in his tool satchel. The gate sergeant nearly searches the satchel before Maren's fabricated delivery order turns him away. Emotional beat: triumph laced with guilt over endangering friends.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Mail Coach
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. On the coach, Paloma sits across from the magistrate's wife, who chats amiably about the eviction as if discussing weather, revealing her complicity and her loneliness. A guard inspects luggage; the bob passes as scrap brass. Emotional beat: disillusionment—corruption is banal, woven into ordinary courtesy.

chapters.title: The Clerk's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. The third checkpoint proves impassable by trickery: the clerk knows every courier by face. Paloma's plan dies in the post office doorway, and he learns the Ashcombes have summoned him for questioning at dawn. Maren proposes the unthinkable—deliver the letter himself, openly, and testify. Emotional beat: despair giving way to a harder courage.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Man Himself
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Climax. Rather than smuggle the letter, Paloma walks into the magistrate's chambers, lays it on the desk, and gives his true name. The confrontation cracks open: the clerk, shown the ledger's forgery, defects; the journalist arrives with witnesses from the settlement. Ashcombe's power shatters publicly as the master clock above them stops mid-chime. Emotional beat: fear burned away into defiant clarity.

chapters.title: Paloma Fairweather
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Weeks later, the trial concluded and the settlement's deeds restored, Paloma—no longer Ansel—apprentices anew with a clockmaker in the river town, his papers honest this time. Maren visits with bread; Ivo sends letters. The observatory clock runs again under new hands. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not forged; time, finally, on his side.
